claim: Context engineering is defined by LangChain as 'the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step,' analogous to Karpathy's framing of the LLM context window as an operating system's RAM.
stance_target: foundational definition of context engineering for agent systems
quoted_support: [Context engineering is the] "...delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step."

claim: Four context-engineering strategies -- write, select, compress, isolate -- describe the common ways production agent systems manage context window content.
stance_target: taxonomy of context engineering strategies for agent systems
scope_conditions: LangChain synthesis of agent products and papers, 2025
quoted_support: We group common strategies for agent context engineering into four buckets — write, select, compress, and isolate — and give examples of each from review of some popular agent products and papers.

claim: Anthropic's multi-agent researcher's LeadResearcher saves its plan to persistent memory because the context window gets truncated once it exceeds 200,000 tokens.
stance_target: write-context (scratchpad/memory) strategies are necessary to survive hard context-window truncation limits in long-running agent tasks
quoted_support: The LeadResearcher begins by thinking through the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context, since if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated and it is important to retain the plan.

claim: Multi-agent isolation (sub-agents exploring in parallel with their own context windows) can outperform single-agent approaches, but costs up to 15x more tokens than a single chat interaction, per Anthropic's own reporting.
stance_target: multi-agent 'software factory' architectures trade cost efficiency for capability -- a direct input to the cost/resource optimization pillar
quoted_support: [Subagents operate] in parallel with their own context windows, exploring different aspects of the question simultaneously... the challenges with multi-agent include token use (e.g., up to 15× more tokens than chat as reported by Anthropic).

claim: Applying RAG to tool descriptions (retrieving only relevant tools for a task instead of exposing the full tool catalog) improves tool-selection accuracy by roughly 3-fold, per cited research.
stance_target: select-context strategies (dynamic tool retrieval) materially improve agent reliability over static large tool catalogs
scope_conditions: cited research papers on agent tool selection, 2025
quoted_support: One approach is to apply RAG (retrieval augmented generation) to tool descriptions in order to fetch only the most relevant tools for a task. Some recent papers have shown that this improve tool selection accuracy by 3-fold.

claim: Claude Code automatically triggers 'auto-compact' summarization once a session exceeds 95% of the context window, compressing the full user-agent interaction trajectory.
stance_target: compress-context strategy implementation example in a production coding agent
scope_conditions: Claude Code product behavior, as of 2025
quoted_support: Claude Code runs "auto-compact" after you exceed 95% of the context window and it will summarize the full trajectory of user-agent interactions.

claim: Drew Breunig identifies four distinct failure modes from long/accumulated agent context: Context Poisoning (hallucination entering context), Context Distraction (context overwhelming training), Context Confusion (superfluous context influencing response), and Context Clash (parts of context disagreeing).
stance_target: zero-hallucination/quality-control pillar requires explicit context-management controls, not just bigger context windows
scope_conditions: Drew Breunig analysis, cited by LangChain 2025
quoted_support: Context Poisoning: When a hallucination makes it into the context. Context Distraction: When the context overwhelms the training. Context Confusion: When superfluous context influences the response. Context Clash: When parts of the context disagree.
